method: S1 is the open RACGP AJGP case study of October 2025, fetched and checked verbatim (16 claims, 5 of them doses). It covers PROSTATITIS ONLY; a targeted search found no open current Australian source for the BPH drug half, so that half is entirely licensed and unquoted, and the guideline says so where it matters. A1 is AMH across four pages, paraphrased, no passage reproduced and no source_text stored. THE TWO SOURCES GIVE DIFFERENT DURATIONS for chronic bacterial prostatitis -- A1 says 4 weeks, S1 says 6 weeks -- and both are stated with attribution rather than averaged. Neither class monograph carries numeric doses for the individual alpha-blockers or 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors; those monographs were NOT retrieved and the gap is recorded rather than filled from memory.

claims.claim: Prostatitis is classified by the National Institutes of Health system into four types: acute bacterial prostatitis, chronic bacterial prostatitis, chronic prostatitis or chronic pelvic pain syndrome, and asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis
claims.source_text: Prostatitis refers to the condition of prostate gland inflammation, which is classified as per the internationally accepted National Institutes of Health Classification System detailed in Table 1. 1 ABP is a subtype of prostatitis, characterised by rapid onset of symptomatic prostate inflammation caused by bacterial invasion.

claims.claim: S1 gives acute bacterial prostatitis as up to 10% of cases, chronic bacterial prostatitis under 5%, chronic prostatitis or chronic pelvic pain syndrome over 90%, and asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis as rare
claims.source_text: Proportion of cases 3,4 Up to 10% <5% >90% Rare

claims.claim: S1 describes acute bacterial prostatitis as acute development of irritative and obstructive urinary symptoms with systemic symptoms and pain, chronic bacterial prostatitis as infection persisting beyond a 3-month period, and chronic pelvic pain syndrome as obstructive urinary symptoms without any bacterial infection
claims.source_text: Acute development of irritative and obstructive urinary symptoms, systemic symptoms and pain Symptoms of ABP or remains asymptomatic. Infection persists beyond a 3-month period Obstructive urinary symptoms without any bacterial infection There are no urinary or systemic symptoms, despite prostate inflammation

claims.claim: Acute bacterial prostatitis is a clinical diagnosis, and it is imperative to recognise it because despite shared features with simple UTI and sexually transmissible infection the management approach and complication risks differ
claims.source_text: ABP is a clinical diagnosis, based on the presence of key features, outlined in Table 2. It is imperative to recognise ABP because despite shared features with other pathologies including simple UTI and sexually transmitted infection (STI), the management approach and complication risks differ.

claims.claim: On digital rectal examination in acute bacterial prostatitis the prostate gland is tender, hot and boggy, and pain is poorly localised to the perineum, external genitalia, tip of penis, rectum, suprapubic region or lower back
claims.source_text: Digital rectal examination - prostate gland is tender, hot and boggy 2 … Poorly localised pain - perineal, external genitalia, tip of penis, rectum, suprapubic region to lower back

claims.claim: S1 states that the pre- and post-prostate massage test is contraindicated in the investigation of suspected acute bacterial prostatitis because of the risk of bacteraemia and is reserved only for investigation of suspected chronic bacterial prostatitis
claims.source_text: PPMT - note that this test is contraindicated in the investigation of suspected ABP because of the risk of bacteraemia; this is reserved only for investigation of suspected chronic bacterial prostatitis (refer to Table 4) 4

claims.claim: S1 states that PSA is not a diagnostic criterion for acute bacterial prostatitis but is useful to indicate prostatic involvement which might aid in excluding other differentials, and that PSA is elevated above 4 micrograms per litre in 70% of acute bacterial prostatitis cases
claims.source_text: PSA - not a diagnostic criterion for ABP, rather it is useful to indicate prostatic involvement, which might aid in excluding other differentials. 1 PSA is elevated (>4 µg/L) in 70% of ABP cases 1

claims.claim: A first void urine specimen for PCR is used to detect Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae in acute bacterial prostatitis caused by an STI, and transrectal or bladder ultrasound is indicated only if acute urinary retention is suspected
claims.source_text: First void urine specimen (PCR) - Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoea, in a ABP caused by an STI 3 … Transrectal or bladder ultrasound - indicated only if acute urinary retention is suspected to determine whether bladder emptying is incomplete 4

claims.claim: S1 states that acute bacterial prostatitis can be managed safely in the community if the patient is haemodynamically stable without signs of severe infection, with trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 14 days as first-line therapy, although the choice of antibiotic should be guided by susceptibility testing and patient factors including allergies
claims.source_text: ABP can be managed safely in the community if the patient is haemodynamically stable without signs of severe infection (Table 2), with Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 14 days, as first-line therapy. 7 However, the choice of antibiotic should be guided by susceptibility testing and account for patient factors including allergies.

claims.claim: S1 lists indications for urgent hospital referral for intravenous antimicrobial therapy as being severely unwell or having signs of sepsis, recent transrectal or transurethral prostatic manipulation, urinary retention which will additionally require catheterisation, inability to tolerate oral antibiotics, and antibiotic resistance
claims.source_text: Urgent hospital referral should be made for patients who meet any of the following indications for intravenous antimicrobial therapy: 7 - severely unwell or have signs of sepsis - refer to Table 2 3,5 - recent transrectal or transurethral prostatic manipulation 2 - urinary retention - will additionally require catheterisation 5 - inability to tolerate oral antibiotics 2 - antibiotic resistance. 5

claims.claim: S1 advises that on completion of the initial antibiotic course the response should be reviewed, and an additional 2 to 4 weeks of antimicrobial therapy prescribed if genitourinary or systemic symptoms persist, repeat urine cultures display bacterial growth, or PSA levels remain elevated
claims.source_text: Upon completion of the initial antibiotic course, healthcare practitioners should review the response to treatment. An additional 2-4 weeks of antimicrobial therapy should be prescribed if: 7 - genitourinary or systemic - symptoms persist - repeat urine cultures display bacterial growth - PSA levels remain elevated.

claims.claim: Supportive therapies for acute bacterial prostatitis include antipyretics, anti-inflammatories, alpha-blockers and stool softeners
claims.source_text: Supportive therapies can also be recommended to aid in symptomatic relief, including: 2 - antipyretics - anti-inflammatories - alpha-blockers - stool softeners.

claims.claim: S1 states that chronic bacterial prostatitis is treated with antibiotics for 6 weeks and notes there is lower tissue penetration of antibiotic therapy because of less inflammation compared to acute bacterial prostatitis
claims.source_text: Antibiotics for 6 weeks There is lower tissue penetration of antibiotic therapy because of less inflammation compared to ABP

claims.claim: S1 gives chronic pelvic pain syndrome features as penile pain, inguinal pain, pudendal discomfort, prostate hyperplasia and bladder outlet obstruction, treated with alpha-1 blockers and phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, and notes it can impact mental health and functioning causing insomnia and depression
claims.source_text: Penile pain, inguinal pain, pudendal discomfort, prostate hyperplasia, bladder outlet obstruction PPMT - no bacteraemia detected Alpha-1 blockers, phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors Can impact mental health and functioning causing insomnia and depression

claims.claim: S1 gives epididymitis as a complication treated with an oral quinolone for 14 to 21 days, with ultrasound to rule out testicular torsion, noting that if untreated it can narrow the passage sperm must pass and contribute to infertility
claims.source_text: Epididymitis 1 Urethral damage, genital swelling, tenderness Ultrasound - to rule out testicular torsion Oral quinolone for 14-21 days If untreated it can narrow the passage sperm must pass and contribute to infertility

claims.claim: S1 gives prostate abscess as a complication indicated by elevated inflammation markers despite antibiotic treatment, investigated by transrectal ultrasound, with surgical drainage if greater than 1 cm
claims.source_text: Prostate abscess Elevated inflammation markers despite antibiotic treatment 3 Transrectal ultrasound 6 If >1 cm, perform surgical drain (TURP) 6
